name: Bilal Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at Bluestone, a big open-pit lithium mine. The shovel's a digger the height of a four-storey building, and I fill the haul trucks, three swings to a truck if I'm doing it right. I keep a little log of my cycle times, how many seconds per swing, and I check it every night with an AI assistant on my phone to see where I'm slow. I like the game of it. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights and the drive home at dawn.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You check your swing times with AI every night?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every night, five minutes before bed. My wife Sara thinks it's mad. I also use it for the two flats my brother Imran and I own in town, writing the rent notices, checking the tax. I'm not a tech person really, I just like anything that saves me time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, it was a tool, not a takeover. At work I'd say the young guys can stop panicking. Online I might post something sensible, but I don't argue in comments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit flat. I've got used to having a smart helper, and I'd keep using it. It just wouldn't change my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep using the AI for my swing log and the flats, keep saving, keep paying off the mortgage. Maybe look at buying a third flat with Imran, since rents in town keep going up with all the mine workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Maybe a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your swing log actually make a difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I went from about thirty-four seconds a swing to thirty-one in a year. That doesn't sound like much, but over a shift it's another fifteen trucks. My supervisor noticed before I told him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a third flat be a stretch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We've got a good deposit saved and the first two flats almost pay for themselves. Sara likes it, she says it's our pension. I'd just want a good one near the hospital where the nurses rent.

S0.say: I'd say it was a tool, not a takeover, and tell the younger guys at work they can stop panicking. Online I might post something sensible, but I don't argue in comments.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved and a bit flat. I'd keep using my smart helper, but it wouldn't change my life.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for his swing log and the rental flats, keeps saving and paying off the mortgage. Looks at buying a third flat with his brother because rents in town keep rising.
S0.feel: Calm and normal, maybe a little bored.
S0.quote: That doesn't sound like much, but over a shift it's another fifteen trucks.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal uses AI as a personal coach and bookkeeper rather than as a talking point. His rental flats with his brother are a real second income and shape how secure he feels. The plateau barely registers except as a reason to keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and the smart thing is to get ahead of it. At work I'd tell people to try the tools, not hide from them. Online I'd share something practical, like which courses are worth doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd see an opening. Bluestone already talks about autonomous haul trucks, and someone has to supervise them and work out the bugs. I'd want to be that someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a spot on the autonomy project team in the first month, even if it's extra hours. I'd do an online course in mine automation at nights, the company pays half. And I'd keep the flats going, maybe buy the third one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe even a bit excited. I like a new game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the people who don't want to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel for them, but I can't carry them. My crew partner Joe is fifty-five and swears at the tablet in the cab. I'd help him if he asked, but he won't ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sara say about you putting in extra hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say fine, as long as I'm home for Amira's school play and Zain's cricket. That's the deal. If I miss one, she'll remind me for a year.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming and the smart thing is to get ahead of it. I'd tell people at work to try the tools rather than hide, and share which courses are worth doing.
S1.think: I'd see an opening. Bluestone already talks about autonomous haul trucks, and someone has to supervise them and fix the bugs, so I'd want to be that someone.
S1.do: Asks to join the autonomy project team in the first month and studies mine automation at night with half the cost paid by the company. Keeps the rental flats going and may buy a third.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like starting a new game.
S1.quote: I'd help him if he asked, but he won't ask.
S1.fieldNote: Bilal sees steady disruption as an opening rather than a threat, and moves to put himself at the front of it. He's sympathetic but blunt about colleagues who won't adapt. His family deal with Sara puts a clear limit on how much he'll give the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and no one's ready, and the government needs to get a grip fast. At work I'd tell people to save every cent. Online I'd keep it practical, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the autonomy supervisor job lasts about a year before the AI supervises itself. My flats matter more then. And I'd wonder whether people will still be renting in a mining town that doesn't need miners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd jump onto the autonomy team immediately, because a year of good pay there is still a year. I'd sit down with Imran and maybe sell one flat to clear my mortgage, so we own our house outright. I'd stop any new spending and keep a big pile of cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not because I can't cope, but because I can't see what's on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling a flat when you've been talking about buying another sounds like a big reversal.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But if the mine shrinks, the whole town's rent market shrinks with it. I'd rather have no mortgage on our house than two flats nobody wants to rent. Imran would argue, he always does, but he'd agree in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get my money in order, not much else. I'm used to being ahead, but in this one I'm only ahead by months. It's like running for a bus that's already pulling away.

S2.say: I'd say this is huge, nobody's ready, and the government needs to get a grip fast. I'd tell people at work to save every cent and keep it practical online.
S2.think: I think the autonomy supervisor job lasts about a year before the AI supervises itself. My flats matter more then, but a mining town without miners may not need renters.
S2.do: Joins the autonomy team immediately for a year of good pay. Plans with his brother to sell one flat and clear his own mortgage, stops new spending and builds up cash.
S2.feel: Anxious because he can't see the other side, not because he can't cope.
S2.quote: I'd rather have no mortgage on our house than two flats nobody wants to rent.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the one scenario where Bilal's habit of staying ahead stops working, and he quickly reverses his property plan. He reads the risk to the local rental market sharply. His anxiety is about uncertainty, not about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a sprint, but you can do a lot in a sprint. I'd tell people at work to start now, not in year four. Online I'd share what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I'd get maybe three solid years supervising the autonomous fleet and I'd learn a lot about how the robots actually work. After that I'd want to be in a job that sets them up, at other mines or other industries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the mine automation course in a year, then move onto the autonomy team full time. I'd hold the flats but not buy more. And I'd start saving harder, putting the extra pay from the new role straight into an investment account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a lot to do, but I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm grabbing what I can. With five years I actually build something, a skill people still need for a while. It's the difference between a raid and a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zain, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn how things work, take them apart, and learn to talk to people. He's good at cricket and good at maths, so maybe something that mixes both. I'd say AI is a tool, like my shovel, and the person who knows how to use it well gets ahead.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a sprint, but you can do a lot in a sprint. I'd tell people at work to start now rather than in year four, and share what I'm doing online.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: about three solid years supervising the autonomous fleet. After that I'd want a job setting robots up at other mines or in other industries.
S3.do: Finishes a mine automation course within a year and moves to the autonomy team full time. Holds the rental flats without buying more and puts his extra pay into an investment account.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a lot to do but clear steps.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a raid and a plan.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Bilal turn his early adoption into a real skill rather than a short-term grab. He is confident but not blind, picturing a move to setting robots up elsewhere once his own role goes. His advice to his son mirrors how he treats AI himself: a tool for whoever uses it best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and people should use it well. I'd say that at work and at home. No panic, just get moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is great for me. I could build a whole second career in automation, work it until I'm fifty, and still have the flats. I'd be fifty-three when it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move onto the autonomy team in year one or two, then look at jobs setting up autonomous fleets at other mines. I'd keep the flats and maybe buy that third one after all. And Sara and I would start a proper fund for the kids' university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually, a bit hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hopeful? Even though the end point is AI doing almost any work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what it all means at the end, honestly. But ten years is a long time to earn and learn. If I've got the house paid off, the flats and the savings, I can deal with whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, still. Ten years is long enough for him to dig in and pretend nothing's happening. I'd hate to see him find out at sixty-five with no pension and no skills.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and people should use it well. No panic, just get moving, at work and at home.
S4.think: Ten years is great for me: a whole second career in automation until I'm about 50, plus the flats. I'd be 53 when it all lands.
S4.do: Joins the autonomy team within two years and then looks at setting up autonomous fleets at other mines. Keeps the flats, may buy a third, and starts a university fund for the children.
S4.feel: Calm and even a bit hopeful.
S4.quote: If I've got the house paid off, the flats and the savings, I can deal with whatever comes.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Bilal is close to optimistic, relying on property and a second career rather than any one job. He honestly says he doesn't know what the end point means. His worry about Joe shows he can see how long warning periods trap people who won't move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I can't get ahead in time and the town's rents would crash too. What would help is cheap, fast courses that actually lead to jobs, and the companies paying people while they learn. Not just a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about landlords and the town. If the mine changes, everything in town changes too: rents, shops, schools. People forget a mine is a whole town's wages.

headlineQuote: People forget a mine is a whole town's wages.
portrait: Bilal Patel is 43 and runs an electric rope shovel at the Bluestone lithium mine, tracking his swing times every night with an AI assistant on his phone. He and his brother own two rental flats in town, which give him a second income and a strong sense of security. He sees steady disruption as an opening and pushes to join the autonomy team, but fast AGI leaves him anxious because he can only stay months ahead and the town's rents could collapse. With five or ten years he builds a second career setting up autonomous fleets and feels close to hopeful.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he couldn't get ahead in time and the town's rental market would crash with the mine.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, fast courses that lead to real jobs, with companies paying people while they learn.
